claim: Actomyosin contractility and planar cell polarity (PCP) interact in post-mitotic Ciona notochord cells to self-assemble and reposition actomyosin rings.
source: In this report, we demonstrate that actomyosin contractility and planar cell polarity (PCP) interact in post-mitotic Ciona notochord cells to self-assemble and reposition actomyosin rings, which play an essential role for cell elongation.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data including drug treatments, genetic manipulations, and live imaging.

claim: Actomyosin rings play an essential role for cell elongation in Ciona notochord cells.
source: In this report, we demonstrate that actomyosin contractility and planar cell polarity (PCP) interact in post-mitotic Ciona notochord cells to self-assemble and reposition actomyosin rings, which play an essential role for cell elongation.
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited and experimental observations showing that ring positioning affects cell elongation.

claim: Actomyosin rings always form at the cells' anterior edge before migrating towards the center as contractility increases.
source: Intriguingly, rings always form at the cells′ anterior edge before migrating towards the center as contractility increases, reflecting a novel dynamical property of the cortex.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data showing ring formation and migration patterns.

claim: The migration of rings from anterior to center reflects a novel dynamical property of the cortex.
source: Intriguingly, rings always form at the cells′ anterior edge before migrating towards the center as contractility increases, reflecting a novel dynamical property of the cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed ring migration behavior.

claim: There is a tug-of-war between contractility and PCP in positioning actomyosin rings.
source: Our drug and genetic manipulations uncover a tug-of-war between contractility, which localizes cortical flows toward the equator and PCP, which tries to reposition them.
evidence: Supported by blebbistatin treatment experiments and aimless mutant analysis showing opposing effects.

claim: Contractility localizes cortical flows toward the equator.
source: Our drug and genetic manipulations uncover a tug-of-war between contractility, which localizes cortical flows toward the equator and PCP, which tries to reposition them.
evidence: Demonstrated through blebbistatin experiments showing that reducing contractility causes anterior shift of rings.

claim: PCP tries to reposition cortical flows away from the equator.
source: Our drug and genetic manipulations uncover a tug-of-war between contractility, which localizes cortical flows toward the equator and PCP, which tries to reposition them.
evidence: Supported by aimless mutant experiments showing randomized ring positioning when PCP is disrupted.

claim: The Ciona notochord is composed of 40 post-mitotic cells arranged in a single file after convergent/extension.
source: The Ciona notochord is a transient embryonic structure, which is composed of 40 post-mitotic cells that are arranged in a single file after convergent/extension (C/E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ciona notochord anatomy.

claim: Following convergent/extension, coin-shaped notochord cells undergo continuous elongation along the anterior–posterior axis.
source: Following C/E, the coin-shaped cells undergo continuous elongation along the anterior–posterior axis (Cloney, 1964; Miyamoto and Crowther, 1985; Jiang and Smith, 2007; Dong et al., 2009), acquiring a drum shape (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by cited literature and Figure 1A showing cell shape changes.

claim: Elongating notochord cells acquire a drum shape.
source: Following C/E, the coin-shaped cells undergo continuous elongation along the anterior–posterior axis (Cloney, 1964; Miyamoto and Crowther, 1985; Jiang and Smith, 2007; Dong et al., 2009), acquiring a drum shape (Figure 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A and supported by cited literature.

claim: An actomyosin contractile ring is present in the basal equator of notochord cells.
source: Our previous studies show that an actomyosin contractile ring is present in the basal equator (Dong et al., 2011) and produces a circumferential constriction.
evidence: Supported by previous study cited (Dong et al., 2011).

claim: The actomyosin contractile ring produces a circumferential constriction.
source: Our previous studies show that an actomyosin contractile ring is present in the basal equator (Dong et al., 2011) and produces a circumferential constriction.
evidence: Supported by previous study and observable in figures.

claim: The force generated by the constriction is transmitted three dimensionally from the basal cortex towards anterior and posterior lateral domains through an incompressible cytoplasm, driving notochord cell elongation.
source: The force generated by the constriction is transmitted three dimensionally from the basal cortex towards anterior and posterior lateral domains through an incompressible cytoplasm, driving notochord cell elongation (Dong et al., 2011; Sehring et al., 2014) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by cited previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The actomyosin ring is maintained by a bi-directional cortical flow.
source: The actomyosin ring is maintained by a bi-directional cortical flow and is under constant turnover in a manner remarkably similar to that of the cytokinetic ring during cell division.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data and kymograph analysis.

claim: The actomyosin ring is under constant turnover in a manner remarkably similar to that of the cytokinetic ring during cell division.
source: The actomyosin ring is maintained by a bi-directional cortical flow and is under constant turnover in a manner remarkably similar to that of the cytokinetic ring during cell division.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments showing turnover time of 90 seconds.

claim: The position of contractile rings influences notochord cell shape and elongation.
source: The position of contractile rings influences notochord cell shape and elongation.
evidence: Supported by α-actinin mutant analysis showing asymmetric cell shape when ring position is not maintained.

claim: In α-actinin mutants, the ring cannot maintain its position at the equator, and consequently, the cells fail to elongate but acquire an asymmetric shape.
source: For example, in α-actinin mutants, the ring cannot maintain its position at the equator, and consequently, the cells fail to elongate but acquire an asymmetric shape (Sehring et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited previous study (Sehring et al., 2014).

claim: Notochord cells acquire a subtle yet stable anterior/posterior (A/P) polarity.
source: In addition, notochord cells acquire a subtle yet stable anterior/posterior (A/P) polarity: nuclei in all but the most posterior cell become localized at the posterior pole of the cell, while the classical PCP protein prickle is localized at the anterior pole of the cell during the notochord cell elongation (Jiang et al., 2005; Newman-Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited studies showing nuclear and prickle localization patterns.

claim: Nuclei in all but the most posterior notochord cell become localized at the posterior pole of the cell.
source: In addition, notochord cells acquire a subtle yet stable anterior/posterior (A/P) polarity: nuclei in all but the most posterior cell become localized at the posterior pole of the cell, while the classical PCP protein prickle is localized at the anterior pole of the cell during the notochord cell elongation (Jiang et al., 2005; Newman-Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited studies and observable in figures.

claim: The classical PCP protein prickle is localized at the anterior pole of the cell during notochord cell elongation.
source: In addition, notochord cells acquire a subtle yet stable anterior/posterior (A/P) polarity: nuclei in all but the most posterior cell become localized at the posterior pole of the cell, while the classical PCP protein prickle is localized at the anterior pole of the cell during the notochord cell elongation (Jiang et al., 2005; Newman-Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited studies and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Before convergent/extension (11.5 hpf), actin was uniformly localized in the basal cortex, with high concentration at notochord cell–cell contacts.
source: Before C/E (11.5 hpf, hours post fertilization), actin was uniformly localized in the basal cortex, with high concentration at notochord cell–cell contacts (arrows in Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with arrows indicating cell-cell contacts.

claim: During cell intercalation (16.5 hpf), the low and evenly distributed actin in the basal cortex was replaced by patches of cortical actin accumulations close to the anterior pole.
source: During cell intercalation (16.5 hpf), when the cells start to align into a column, the low and evenly distributed actin in the basal cortex was replaced by patches of cortical actin accumulations close to the anterior pole (white arrowheads in Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with white arrowheads indicating actin patches.

claim: With the alignment of the cells into a column (17 hpf), actin patches connected into an actin ring spanning the entire circumference of the basal domain next to the anterior pole of the coin-shaped cell.
source: With the alignment of the cells into a column (17 hpf), these actin patches connected into an actin ring spanning the entire circumference of the basal domain next to the anterior pole of the coin-shaped cell (yellow arrowheads and intensity graph in Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with yellow arrowheads and intensity measurements.

claim: The early anterior ring observed in coin-shaped cells is the precursor of the equatorial ring.
source: Time-lapse recordings revealed that this early anterior ring observed in coin-shaped cells is the precursor of the equatorial ring (Video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse recordings in Video 1.

claim: While the cells elongated, the ring relocated from the anterior pole to the equator of the cells.
source: While the cells elongated, the ring relocated from the anterior pole to the equator of the cells (white arrowheads in Figure 1E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: The length between the ring and the posterior pole grew only minimally during ring relocation.
source: While the length between the ring and the posterior pole grew only minimally, the length between the anterior pole and the ring increased steadily, until the distance from the ring to both poles was similar (Figure 1F).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The length between the anterior pole and the ring increased steadily during ring relocation, until the distance from the ring to both poles was similar.
source: While the length between the ring and the posterior pole grew only minimally, the length between the anterior pole and the ring increased steadily, until the distance from the ring to both poles was similar (Figure 1F).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Concomitantly with ring relocation and cell elongation, the ring width increased.
source: Concomitantly with ring relocation and cell elongation, the ring width increased (Figure 1F′).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 1F'.

claim: Myosin filaments formed a circumferential ring in the anterior basal cortex at the end of convergent/extension.
source: Myosin filaments (labeled with myosin regulatory light chain fused to mCherry, mCherry-MRLC) also formed a circumferential ring in the anterior basal cortex at the end of C/E.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The myosin ring relocated to the equator similarly to the actin ring.
source: Similarly to the actin ring, the myosin ring subsequently relocated to the equator (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), where it remained for the rest of the elongation process.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with myosin II ATPase inhibitor blebbistatin at the onset of cell elongation prevented both cell elongation and the posterior relocation of the actin ring.
source: Treatment with myosin II ATPase inhibitor blebbistatin at the onset of cell elongation prevented both cell elongation and the posterior relocation of the actin ring; instead, the actin ring remained at the anterior end of the cells (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1G,H comparing DMSO control to blebbistatin treatment.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment at the onset of cell elongation caused the actin ring to remain at the anterior end of the cells.
source: Treatment with myosin II ATPase inhibitor blebbistatin at the onset of cell elongation prevented both cell elongation and the posterior relocation of the actin ring; instead, the actin ring remained at the anterior end of the cells (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Notochord cells in blebbistatin-treated embryos ceased to elongate when treated after substantial elongation had occurred.
source: At this stage, notochord cells in drug-treated embryos ceased to elongate (Figure 2A,A′).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A,A'.

claim: The equatorial actin ring present at the start of blebbistatin treatment was lost and an anterior accumulation of actin appeared.
source: Surprisingly, the equatorial actin ring present at the start of the treatment (white arrowheads in Figure 2A) was lost; instead, we observed an anterior accumulation of actin (yellow arrowheads in Figure 2A′), similar to the anterior concentration of actin in coin-shaped cells.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2A,A' with white and yellow arrowheads.

claim: The effect of blebbistatin is reversible.
source: The effect of blebbistatin is reversible (Figure 2B,B′): notochord cells were able to elongate significantly following a 60-min wash, and the cortical actin ring returned from the anterior edge of the cells to the equator.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B,B' demonstrating recovery after wash.

claim: Following a 60-min wash after blebbistatin treatment, notochord cells were able to elongate significantly and the cortical actin ring returned from the anterior edge of the cells to the equator.
source: The effect of blebbistatin is reversible (Figure 2B,B′): notochord cells were able to elongate significantly following a 60-min wash, and the cortical actin ring returned from the anterior edge of the cells to the equator.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B,B'.

claim: High-speed time-lapse recordings revealed a migration of the cortical actin ring from the equator to the anterior pole during blebbistatin treatment.
source: High-speed time-lapse recordings revealed a migration of the cortical actin ring from the equator to the anterior pole (Figure 2C,C′; Video 2), mirroring exactly the reverse sequence of migration of the ring towards the center in normal development.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C,C' and Video 2.

claim: The blebbistatin-induced anterior shift of the ring mirrors exactly the reverse sequence of migration of the ring towards the center in normal development.
source: High-speed time-lapse recordings revealed a migration of the cortical actin ring from the equator to the anterior pole (Figure 2C,C′; Video 2), mirroring exactly the reverse sequence of migration of the ring towards the center in normal development.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of normal development and blebbistatin treatment dynamics.

claim: The front of the ring moved at a velocity of 91.8 ± 10.5 nm/min during blebbistatin treatment.
source: The front of the ring moved at a velocity of 91.8 ± 10.5 nm/min (n = 10).
evidence: Measured from time-lapse recordings.

claim: The speed of the ring shift was blebbistatin dose dependent.
source: The speed of the shift was blebbistatin dose dependent; halving the blebbistatin concentration reduced the velocity significantly to 27 ± 0.5 nm/min (n = 10; p < 0.0001).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing velocities at different blebbistatin concentrations.

claim: Halving the blebbistatin concentration reduced the ring shift velocity significantly to 27 ± 0.5 nm/min.
source: The speed of the shift was blebbistatin dose dependent; halving the blebbistatin concentration reduced the velocity significantly to 27 ± 0.5 nm/min (n = 10; p < 0.0001).
evidence: Measured from time-lapse recordings at half blebbistatin concentration.

claim: The ring width stayed constant when it shifted anteriorly during blebbistatin treatment.
source: The ring width stayed constant when it shifted anteriorly (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After the ring contacted the lateral domain, the posterior edge of the ring continued to move anteriorly at an increasing speed of 191.6 ± 21.4 nm/min.
source: Instead, after the ring contacted the lateral domain (red line in Figure 2D), the posterior edge of the ring continued to move anteriorly at an increasing speed of 191.6 ± 21.4 nm/min (n = 10), so that the width of the ring narrowed (Figure 2D), until the entire ring disappeared at the position of the lateral domain (Video 2).
evidence: Measured from time-lapse recordings and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The width of the ring narrowed after contacting the lateral domain until the entire ring disappeared at the position of the lateral domain.
source: Instead, after the ring contacted the lateral domain (red line in Figure 2D), the posterior edge of the ring continued to move anteriorly at an increasing speed of 191.6 ± 21.4 nm/min (n = 10), so that the width of the ring narrowed (Figure 2D), until the entire ring disappeared at the position of the lateral domain (Video 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: The cell length did not significantly change during the ring shifting process.
source: The cell length did not significantly change during this process (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; n = 10).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Talin concentrated at the cell equator slightly after the ring had been established centrally.
source: Live imaging showed that talin concentrated at the cell equator slightly after the ring had been established centrally (data not shown), suggesting that talin actually responds to cortical repositioning rather than driving it.
evidence: Observed through live imaging experiments.

claim: Talin responds to cortical repositioning rather than driving it.
source: Live imaging showed that talin concentrated at the cell equator slightly after the ring had been established centrally (data not shown), suggesting that talin actually responds to cortical repositioning rather than driving it.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal sequence of ring formation and talin localization.

claim: Upon blebbistatin treatment of already established central rings, cortical actin was shifted to the anterior pole while talin lagged behind at the equatorial position.
source: Upon blebbistatin treatment of already established central rings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), whereas the cortical actin was shifted to the anterior pole (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A′), talin lagged behind at the equatorial position (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B′).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Not all components of the ring are shifted by blebbistatin.
source: This result suggests not all components of the ring are shifted by blebbistatin.
evidence: Inferred from the differential behavior of actin and talin during blebbistatin treatment.

claim: Circumferentially oriented actin filament bundles from the anterior and posterior edges of the ring continued to flow towards the equator during blebbistatin treatment.
source: The kymograph unveiled a persistence of this dynamics within the ring in blebbistatin-treated embryos: circumferentially oriented actin filament bundles (arrows in Figure 2E; further examples are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) from the anterior and posterior edges of the ring continued to flow towards the equator, which itself was shifting anteriorly (dashed line in Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown in kymographs in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the first 15 min of blebbistatin treatment, the filament bundles moved at a velocity of 7.62 ± 0.78 nm/s, which was significantly slower than the velocity in control cells (29.92 nm/s).
source: In the first 15 min of blebbistatin treatment, the filament bundles moved at a velocity of 7.62 ± 0.78 nm/s (n = 18), which was significantly slower than the velocity in control cells (DMSO-treated cells) (29.92 nm/s, n = 10; p < 0.001), where the filaments moved towards a stationary equator.
evidence: Measured from kymograph analysis.

claim: Continued exposure to blebbistatin further reduced filament movement velocity to 3.92 ± 0.9 nm/s within the next 15 min.
source: Continued exposure to blebbistatin further reduced filament movement. Within the next 15 min, the velocity decreased significantly to 3.92 ± 0.9 nm/s (n = 22; p = 0.004).
evidence: Measured from kymograph analysis.

claim: The deceleration of the filament bundles resulted in a flattening of their trajectories in the kymograph.
source: The deceleration of the filament bundles resulted in a flattening of their trajectories in the kymograph.
evidence: Observable in kymographs and quantified by angle measurements.

claim: Measurement of the angles of filament bundles revealed a reduction from 39° to 3° within 30 min of blebbistatin treatment.
source: Measurement of the angles of filament bundles revealed a reduction from 39° to 3° within 30 min of blebbistatin treatment (Figure 2E′,F).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 2E',F.

claim: After 31.1 ± 1.36 min of blebbistatin treatment, directed movement of filament bundles towards the center of the ring ceased.
source: After 31.1 ± 1.36 min (n = 20), directed movement of filament bundles towards the center of the ring (the moving equator) ceased, and only filament bundles moving nearly parallel to the direction of the shifting ring could be observed (yellow arrowheads, Figure 2E).
evidence: Measured from kymograph analysis and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is no statistical difference in either velocities or angles between anterior- and posterior-directed filament bundles at any time.
source: There is no statistical difference in either velocities or angles between anterior- and posterior-directed filament bundles at any time.
evidence: Statistical analysis of measured velocities and angles.

claim: For control embryos, the FRAP recovery curve was well fitted by a single exponential, yielding a characteristic turnover rate of 90 s ± 3 s.
source: For control embryos, the recovery curve was well fitted by a single exponential (Figure 2G), yielding a characteristic turnover rate of 90 s ± 3 s.
evidence: FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the shifting ring with blebbistatin treatment, fluorescence recovered, indicating a persistent cortical flow of actin elements from outside the ring towards its center.
source: In the shifting ring with blebbistatin treatment, fluorescence also recovered, indicating a persistent cortical flow of actin elements from outside the ring towards its center.
evidence: FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: After blebbistatin treatment, the FRAP dynamics contained two characteristic recovery times: a fast one similar to the control, and a much slower one of 7.8 ± 0.6 min.
source: Interestingly, the dynamics could no longer be fitted by a single exponential, as it contained two characteristic recovery times: a fast one, very similar to the control, and a much slower one of 7.8 ± 0.6 min (Figure 2G).
evidence: FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Prolonged treatment with blebbistatin (>1 hr) led to the complete disappearance of the actin ring.
source: Prolonged treatment with blebbistatin (>1 hr) led to the complete disappearance of the actin ring.
evidence: Observed in time-lapse recordings shown in Figure 2H,J and Videos 3,4.

claim: When the first ring was nearly gone, a new actin ring formed.
source: Surprisingly, when the first ring was nearly gone, a new actin ring formed (Figure 2H, Video 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2H and Video 3.

claim: At the time point the first ring disappeared, the second ring emerged.
source: A kymograph generated from the time-lapse reveals that the two rings overlapped in time only transiently: at the time point the first ring disappeared, the second ring emerged (Figure 2I).
evidence: Shown in kymograph in Figure 2I.

claim: The first ring disappeared after 106.67 ± 6.06 min of blebbistatin treatment.
source: While the first ring disappeared after 106.67 ± 6.06 min of blebbistatin treatment (n = 6), the second ring had a significantly shorter dwelling time of only 61.33 ± 7.81 min (p = 0.001) before it disappeared at the anterior edge of the cells.
evidence: Measured from time-lapse recordings.

claim: The second ring had a significantly shorter dwelling time of only 61.33 ± 7.81 min before it disappeared at the anterior edge of the cells.
source: While the first ring disappeared after 106.67 ± 6.06 min of blebbistatin treatment (n = 6), the second ring had a significantly shorter dwelling time of only 61.33 ± 7.81 min (p = 0.001) before it disappeared at the anterior edge of the cells.
evidence: Measured from time-lapse recordings.

claim: The moving actin rings were associated with a morphological bulge at the basal domain during blebbistatin treatment.
source: Intriguingly, we consistently observed the dislodging of the actin rings from the morphological constriction (Figure 2H, arrowheads; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), instead, the moving actin rings were associated with a morphological bulge at the basal domain (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2C′), and cells formed a new circumferential constriction (red arrowheads in Figure 2C′,H) in the wake of the shifting ring.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C',H with yellow arrowheads.

claim: Cells formed a new circumferential constriction in the wake of the shifting ring during blebbistatin treatment.
source: Intriguingly, we consistently observed the dislodging of the actin rings from the morphological constriction (Figure 2H, arrowheads; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), instead, the moving actin rings were associated with a morphological bulge at the basal domain (yellow arrowhead in Figure 2C′), and cells formed a new circumferential constriction (red arrowheads in Figure 2C′,H) in the wake of the shifting ring.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C',H with red arrowheads.

claim: In cells that survived prolonged treatment of blebbistatin with relatively normal morphology, a third ring emerged at the equator after the disappearance of the second ring at the anterior lateral domain.
source: In cells that survived prolonged treatment of blebbistatin with relatively normal morphology, we observed the emergence of a third ring at the equator, after the disappearance of the second ring at the anterior lateral domain (Figure 2J; Video 4).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2J and Video 4.

claim: Halocynthia roretzi notochord follows a remarkably similar early developmental process as in Ciona.
source: To this end, we examined the notochord of the ascidian Halocynthia roretzi, which follows a remarkably similar early developmental process as in Ciona (Figure 3A,B), except at the cell elongation stage, the nuclei are positioned in the center of the cells (asterisks in Figure 3B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: At the cell elongation stage in Halocynthia roretzi, the nuclei are positioned in the center of the cells.
source: To this end, we examined the notochord of the ascidian Halocynthia roretzi, which follows a remarkably similar early developmental process as in Ciona (Figure 3A,B), except at the cell elongation stage, the nuclei are positioned in the center of the cells (asterisks in Figure 3B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3B with asterisks marking nuclei.

claim: A conspicuous circumferential constriction is present at the equator in Halocynthia roretzi notochord cells, which is colocalized with a cortical ring of actin and activated myosin.
source: A conspicuous circumferential constriction is present at the equator, which is colocalized with a cortical ring of actin (Figure 3C) and activated myosin (Figure 3D), whose activity is essential for notochord cell elongation (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Myosin activity is essential for notochord cell elongation in Halocynthia roretzi.
source: A conspicuous circumferential constriction is present at the equator, which is colocalized with a cortical ring of actin (Figure 3C) and activated myosin (Figure 3D), whose activity is essential for notochord cell elongation (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by blebbistatin treatment abolishing elongation in Figure 3E,F.

claim: In Halocynthia roretzi embryos treated with blebbistatin for 3 hr, the actin ring was shifted invariably anteriorly.
source: We next treated embryos with elongating notochord cells with blebbistatin for 3 hr. Similar to what was observed in Ciona, the actin ring was shifted invariably anteriorly (Figure 3G), indicating that the position of the nucleus does not influence the dynamic behavior of the ring.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The position of the nucleus does not influence the dynamic behavior of the ring.
source: We next treated embryos with elongating notochord cells with blebbistatin for 3 hr. Similar to what was observed in Ciona, the actin ring was shifted invariably anteriorly (Figure 3G), indicating that the position of the nucleus does not influence the dynamic behavior of the ring.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that rings shift anteriorly in Halocynthia despite central nuclear position.

claim: In wild-type C. savignyi embryos, elongated notochord cells possess a circumferential actin ring at the cell equator and a posterior nucleus.
source: In wild-type C. savignyi embryos, elongated notochord cells possess a circumferential actin ring at the cell equator and a posterior nucleus (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment shifts the ring towards the anterior pole in wild-type C. savignyi embryos.
source: Blebbistatin treatment shifts the ring towards the anterior pole (Figure 4B), mirroring exactly the events in C. intestinalis.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In aimless embryos, the intercalation of notochord cells is impaired, except in the posterior region where the cells often align into a single file.
source: In aimless embryos, the intercalation of notochord cells (outlined in Figure 4C) is impaired, except in the posterior region where the cells often align into a single file (Jiang et al., 2005).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C and supported by cited study.

claim: In aimless cells, the loss of A/P polarity is evident by the random position of the nuclei.
source: In these cells, the loss of A/P polarity is evident by the random position of the nuclei (Figure 4C insert).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C insert.

claim: In 92% of mock-treated aimless cells, the actin ring is positioned at the equator.
source: In 92% of mock-treated aimless cells in this region, the actin ring is positioned at the equator (Figure 4C insert), showing that equatorial ring positioning is independent from PCP.
evidence: Quantified from Figure 4C and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Equatorial ring positioning is independent from PCP.
source: In 92% of mock-treated aimless cells in this region, the actin ring is positioned at the equator (Figure 4C insert), showing that equatorial ring positioning is independent from PCP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that aimless mutants lacking PCP still position rings at the equator.

claim: Reducing contractility in polarity-deficient mutant cells led to randomized direction of ring shift independent of nuclear localization.
source: However, reducing contractility in polarity-deficient mutant cells led to a dramatically different phenotype: after 60-min blebbistatin treatment, no unidirectional migration towards the anterior was observed. The direction of the shift was randomized and independent of the localization of the nucleus: examples for anterior nucleus and ring, anterior nucleus and posterior ring, posterior nucleus and ring, and posterior nucleus and anterior ring could be found (Figure 4D,D').
evidence: Shown in Figure 4D,D' and quantified in Figure 4E.

claim: In blebbistatin-treated aimless cells, 56% of the cells had the ring positioned at the equator, 18% had anterior rings, and 26% had posterior rings.
source: In 56% of the cells, the ring was still positioned at the equator, and in the rest, the ring migrated either to the anterior or posterior side (18% and 26%) (n = 57) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantified and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A/P polarity by prickle is not necessary for the establishment of an equatorial actin ring.
source: These results imply that A/P polarity by prickle is not necessary for the establishment of an equatorial actin ring; however, it is instrumental for the direction of movement of the ring upon blebbistatin treatment.
evidence: Inferred from aimless mutant experiments showing equatorial rings form without prickle.

claim: A/P polarity by prickle is instrumental for the direction of movement of the ring upon blebbistatin treatment.
source: These results imply that A/P polarity by prickle is not necessary for the establishment of an equatorial actin ring; however, it is instrumental for the direction of movement of the ring upon blebbistatin treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by randomized ring movement in aimless mutants treated with blebbistatin.

claim: If the actomyosin concentration is slightly higher in a given region, then the contractile stress is also locally higher compared to the surroundings.
source: Indeed, if the actomyosin concentration is slightly higher in a given region, then the contractile stress is also locally higher compared to the surroundings.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from active gel models.

claim: A self-reinforcing loop concentrates actomyosin in a single spot at the cortex with filaments flowing towards the ring.
source: Because of this initially small imbalance, surrounding actomyosin fibers flow towards the accumulation, making it even denser and even more contractile (Recho et al., 2013). This self-reinforcing loop, which concentrates actomyosin in a single spot at the cortex with filaments flowing towards the ring, is resisted by their depolymerization and effective diffusion (Figure 5A), which favor a homogenous cortex.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from active gel models, cited from Recho et al., 2013.

claim: Depolymerization and effective diffusion resist the self-reinforcing loop and favor a homogenous cortex.
source: This self-reinforcing loop, which concentrates actomyosin in a single spot at the cortex with filaments flowing towards the ring, is resisted by their depolymerization and effective diffusion (Figure 5A), which favor a homogenous cortex.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the model.

claim: The angle between lateral and basal membrane decreased smoothly and continuously during elongation and ring migration, indicative of an increased basal tension relative to lateral tension.
source: Interestingly, the angle decreased smoothly and continuously during elongation and ring migration, indicative of an increased basal tension relative to lateral tension (Figure 5B), by roughly a factor of 2.5 during the elongation process, and 1.5 during the ring migration process.
evidence: Measured from embryos at various stages and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Basal tension increased by roughly a factor of 2.5 during the elongation process, and 1.5 during the ring migration process.
source: Interestingly, the angle decreased smoothly and continuously during elongation and ring migration, indicative of an increased basal tension relative to lateral tension (Figure 5B), by roughly a factor of 2.5 during the elongation process, and 1.5 during the ring migration process.
evidence: Calculated from angle measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PIV analysis revealed a robust negative linear correlation between local velocity gradients and local actin concentration.
source: When plotting these as a function of local actin concentration, we found a robust negative linear correlation (Figure 5D), which shows that flows are driven by differences in actomyosin concentration, validating quantitatively Equation 3 of our model.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5D from PIV analysis.

claim: Flows are driven by differences in actomyosin concentration.
source: When plotting these as a function of local actin concentration, we found a robust negative linear correlation (Figure 5D), which shows that flows are driven by differences in actomyosin concentration, validating quantitatively Equation 3 of our model.
evidence: Inferred from the negative linear correlation between velocity gradients and actin concentration.

claim: The model predicts a transition between two mechanically stable states of the actin ring: a central position if the contractility χ is large enough, and an anterior position when χ is small enough and the polarity-induced actin flux F dominates.
source: With these final boundary conditions, the dynamical system Equations (1–3) predicts a transition (which is now smooth, see Figure 1 in Appendix 1: the model) between two mechanically stable states of the actin ring: a central position if the contractility χ is large enough, and an anterior position when χ is small enough and the polarity-induced actin flux F dominates.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model.

claim: The model can reproduce quantitatively very well both the velocity and intensity profiles in the entire actin cortex at the late stages of elongation.
source: We found that our model can reproduce quantitatively very well both the velocity and intensity profiles in the entire actin cortex at the late stages of elongation (Figure 5E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5E comparing model predictions to experimental data.

claim: A remaining, albeit small bias in ring position towards the anterior side exists at later stages, both in simulations and in the data.
source: Moreover, we note a remaining, albeit small bias in ring position towards the anterior side, as in the data, showing that an anterior-imbalance remains at the later stages, both in simulations and in the data.
evidence: Observed in both model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The migration speed of the ring is controlled by the dynamics of contractility changes.
source: It should be noted that in our model, the migration speed of the ring is controlled by the dynamics of contractility changes.
evidence: This is a feature of the theoretical model.

claim: The model's dynamical prediction for the positions of the anterior and posterior sides of the ring matched very well the experimental data during normal ring migration.
source: We first examined the dynamics of normal ring migration to the center and verified that our dynamical prediction for the positions of the anterior and posterior sides of the ring matched very well the experimental data (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6B comparing model to experimental data.

claim: The model predicts the size of the actin ring should first increase linearly with the length of the cell, before showing a plateau region for large cell sizes.
source: Moreover, a rather intriguing feature of our model is that it predicts the size of the actin ring should first increase linearly with the length of the cell, before showing a plateau region for large cell sizes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Experimentally measured actin ring width increases linearly with the length of the cell, in very good quantitative agreement with the model.
source: We measured experimentally actin ring width during cell elongation, and found it indeed increases linearly with the length of the cell, in very good quantitative agreement with our model, with all parameters having already been fixed above.
evidence: Measured data shown in Figure 6C matching model predictions.

claim: The model showed good theory-experiment agreement for the shifts of both the anterior and posterior sides of the ring during blebbistatin treatment.
source: This yielded a good theory-experiment agreement for the shifts of both the anterior and posterior sides of the ring (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6B comparing model predictions to blebbistatin treatment data.

claim: The predicted decay of actin velocity from simulations showed excellent quantitative agreement with experimental data.
source: We plotted the predicted decay of actin velocity from our simulations and compared it to the experimental data measured above. Again, we found an excellent quantitative agreement between predictions and data (Figure 6E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6E comparing model to experimental data.

claim: For low polarity and increased contractility (aimless mutant), the ring formed directly in the center of the cell in simulations.
source: To verify the role of PCP in the model, we performed the simulation under the conditions of no polarity and random polarity (Figure 7A): for low polarity and increased contractility (aimless mutant), the ring formed directly in the center of the cell; for low contractility and low, uncoordinated polarity between neighboring cells (aimless mutant with blebbistatin), the actin ring did not have any strong forces positioning it, and was therefore positioned randomly, depending on the strength of the respective anterior and posterior boundary fluxes (see Appendix 5: model predictions for further details).
evidence: This is a prediction from model simulations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: For low contractility and low, uncoordinated polarity between neighboring cells (aimless mutant with blebbistatin), the actin ring was positioned randomly in simulations.
source: To verify the role of PCP in the model, we performed the simulation under the conditions of no polarity and random polarity (Figure 7A): for low polarity and increased contractility (aimless mutant), the ring formed directly in the center of the cell; for low contractility and low, uncoordinated polarity between neighboring cells (aimless mutant with blebbistatin), the actin ring did not have any strong forces positioning it, and was therefore positioned randomly, depending on the strength of the respective anterior and posterior boundary fluxes (see Appendix 5: model predictions for further details).
evidence: This is a prediction from model simulations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Disheveled initially accumulated at the basal membrane, but was relocated to the lateral domains, with a preference for the anterior side (28% ± 9% enrichment compared to the posterior side).
source: As noted earlier, Dsh is a core member of the PCP pathway (Keys et al., 2002), and we found that it initially accumulated at the basal membrane, but was relocated to the lateral domains, with a preference for the anterior side (28% ± 9% enrichment compared to the posterior side, n = 11 cells) (Figure 7B), mirroring the localization of Prickle protein at this stage (Figure 7C) (Jiang, et al., 2005; Newman-Smith, et al., 2015).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7B with quantification.

claim: Disheveled relocation to the lateral domains occurred roughly at the same time as the appearance of the anterior ring (between 19 and 20 hpf).
source: Interestingly, this relocation occurred roughly at the same time as the appearance of the anterior ring (between 19 and 20 hpf).
evidence: Temporal correlation observed from imaging data.

claim: Sufficiently large myosin contractility antagonizes the Prickle/Dishevelled-mediated anterior bias and can self-organize the actin ring in the center of the cell purely by physical forces.
source: This suggests a tug-of-war between contractility and cellular polarity: sufficiently large myosin contractility antagonizes the Prickle/Dishevelled-mediated anterior bias and can self-organize the actin ring in the center of the cell purely by physical forces, as shown by our theoretical analysis (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and theoretical modeling.

claim: The equatorial ring in the notochord cells is established in a spindle-independent manner.
source: Indeed, the equatorial ring in the notochord cells, despite its resemblance to the equatorial ring in cytokinesis, is established in a spindle-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that notochord cells are post-mitotic.

claim: Lifeact-mEGFP and mCherry-UtrCH bind to endogenous actin without interfering with its dynamics.
source: Both Lifeact-mEGFP and mCherry-UtrCH bind to endogenous actin without interfering with its dynamics (Burkel et al., 2007; Riedl et al., 2008) and were shown previously to have the same localization pattern as the endogenous protein in Ciona intestinalis (Sehring et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature.

claim: Lifeact-mEGFP and mCherry-UtrCH have the same localization pattern as the endogenous protein in Ciona intestinalis.
source: Both Lifeact-mEGFP and mCherry-UtrCH bind to endogenous actin without interfering with its dynamics (Burkel et al., 2007; Riedl et al., 2008) and were shown previously to have the same localization pattern as the endogenous protein in Ciona intestinalis (Sehring et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited previous study.
